A Comparison between Technical and Biological Evolution Silvia de Cesare & Vincent Bontems Résumé Dans cet article, De Cesare et Bontems comparent les concepts de progrès et de croissance dans l’évolution technique et dans l’évolution biologique, en proposant une analyse critique des analogies entre ces deux domaines. En s’appuyant sur la philosophie de la technique de Gilbert Simondon et sur la théorie évolutionniste contemporaine, en particulier telle qu’elle est développée par Silvia De Cesare, les auteurs distinguent le progrès pure- ment performatif du progrès authentique. Au niveau technique, Simon- don définit le progrès comme un processus de concrétisation, par lequel les objets deviennent plus cohérents, autosoutenables et mieux couplés à leur milieu, évitant ainsi les évolutions hypertéliques marquées par une spécialisation excessive. Au niveau biologique, l’article montre qu’il est possible de parler de progrès local comme amélioration fonctionnelle adaptative sans recourir à des valeurs morales, tout en en soulignant les limites liées à la fragilité associée à la suradaptation. À des échelles de temps plus longues, l’évoluabilité est proposée comme critère d’un pro- grès organique global, entendu comme la capacité à générer de la diversité face à l’instabilité environnementale. Enfin, le texte dissocie le progrès de la croissance (démographique ou économique), en soutenant que la si- tuation écologique contemporaine exige de repenser le progrès technique indépendamment de l’augmentation quantitative, ouvrant même la voie à l’idée d’un « progrès négatif » orienté vers la soutenabilité, la réduction de la puissance et la préservation de l’évoluabilité des systèmes vivants. Mots-clés : Progrès technique et biologique; Philosophie de la technique; Concrétisation; Évoluabilité; Progrès et croissance. Aion Journal of Philosophy and Science 3, 2026 CONTACT: Silvia de Cesare, Freudenthal Institute, Utrecht University, silviadecesare@gmail. com Vincent Bontems, University Paris-Saclay, vincent.bontems@cea.fr

Silvia de Cesare & Vincent Bontems 45 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 Abstract De Cesare and Bontems compare, in the article, the concepts of prog- ress and growth in technical evolution and biological evolution, offering a critical analysis of the analogies between these two domains. Drawing on Gilbert Simondon’s philosophy of technology and contemporary evo- lutionary theory, especially as developed by Silvia De Cesare, the authors distinguish merely performative progress from genuine progress. On the technical level, Simondon defines progress as a process of concretization, through which objects become more coherent, selfsustaining, and better coupled to their milieu, thereby avoiding hypertelic evolutions marked by excessive specialization. On the biological level, the article shows that it is possible to speak of local progress as adaptive functional improvement without appealing to moral values, while emphasizing its limits due to the fragility associated with overadaptation. At longer timescales, evolv- ability is proposed as a criterion of global organic progress, understood as the capacity to generate diversity in the face of environmental insta- bility. Finally, the text dissociates progress from growth (demographic or economic), arguing that the contemporary ecological situation requires rethinking technical progress independently of quantitative increase, even opening the way for the idea of “negative progress” oriented toward sus- tainability, the reduction of power, and the preservation of the evolvability of living systems. Keywords: Technical and biological progress; Philosophy of technology; Concretization; Evolvability; Progress and growth. Introduction Technical objects and living beings are connected by a very strong and long- standing analogy, which can already be traced back to Aristotle 1. Today, from an evolutionary perspective that has asserted itself since the publication of On the Ori- gin of Species by Charles Darwin 2, one can easily identify a common point between technical objects and living beings: both have an evolutionary history. Indeed, one can speak of biological evolution just as one can speak of technical evolution. In the biological case, it is possible to identify lineages, that is, organisms that represent the same “branch” of the evolutionary tree. In the technical case, one can analogously refer to technical lineages, a concept developed within the framework of French mechanology by Jacques Lafitte 3. In both domains, the technical and the organic, a central question can be posed 1 Canguilhem, G., 2008, Knowledge of Life, New York, Fordham University Press. 2 Darwin, C., 1859, On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, London, John Murray. 3 Lafitte, J., 1932, Réflexions sur la science des machines, Paris, Vrin.

# Page 3^page=3
Progress and Growth 46 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 in the same terms: does it make sense to say that evolutionary change proceeds “to- ward the better”? The question amounts to asking whether the concept of progress, including an axiological component and a descriptive component 4, can legitimately be employed to describe these two types of evolution. The notion of progress as me- liorative evolution was introduced by Francis Bacon in the domain of the sciences and the arts 5. Technical progress proceeds through artifacts that are increasingly ef- ficient according to criteria that remain to be determined. By analogy, in the organic case, the idea of progress designates the fact that the evolution of living beings would imply, in part or in its entirety, a change toward the better 6. Alongside the term progress, another term can be used in relation to both do- mains: that of growth. The term growth is used in biology to describe the increases (in size and in number of cells) that occur during the life history of an organism 7. By extension, it can be used in reference to a population of organisms. Thus, with respect to human beings, the term growth describes the demographic increase of the human population, but also designates, by analogy, economic growth as measured through various indicators. These two types of growth (demographic and economic) are often associated, in one way or another, with technical evolution. In the case of both living beings and technical objects, it is therefore possi- ble to speak of progress and growth. However, it is important to avoid presupposing the validity of the analogies suggested by the use of the same vocabulary. In this contribution, our aim is to clarify the way in which these terms can be understood in their respective domains and thus to assess the validity of the analogies. On the biological side, we will refer to evolutionary theory as it originates in the thought of Charles Darwin, by adopting the conceptual framework recently presented in De Ce- sare 8. On the technical side, we will rely on the analysis of the mode of existence of technical objects developed by the French philosopher Gilbert Simondon 9, whose relevance is increasingly recognized in the field of philosophy of technology 10, draw- ing in particular on the recent synthesis proposed by Bontems 11. We will address the following questions: a) What does “progress” mean in relation to technical evolution as understood within the perspective of Gilbert Simondon? 4 Guffroy, Y., Bontems, V., 2018, “La mécanologie : une lignée technologique francophone ?”, Artefact, 8, pp. 255– 280. 5 Bacon, F., 1605, The Advancement of Learning, London, Thomas Huggins. 6 Ruse, M., 1996, Monad to Man. The Concept of Progress in Evolutionary Biology, Cambridge (MA), Harvard University Press. 7 Wilt, F. (eds.), Cham, Springer. 11 Bontems, V., 2023, Au Nom de l’Innovation. Finalités et modalités de la recherche au XXIe siècle, Paris, Les Belles Lettres.

Silvia de Cesare & Vincent Bontems 47 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 b) What does “progress” mean in the context of evolutionary theory? c) In what way is this organic progress analogous to technical progress sensu Simondon? d) Given that the Simondonian notion of technical progress is detached from that of growth, what can be said of an analogical notion that would apply to both technology and living beings? Before addressing these questions, it will be necessary to begin by highlighting the differences and the common points between technical evolution and biological evolution, which will make it possible to keep in mind the respective specificities of these two domains 1. Differences and common points between technical evolution and biological evolution In her classic study, the philosopher Mary Hesse12 considers analogy to be a sys- tem of relations linking an object or a system of objects (called the source) to another object or system of objects (called the target). Hesse takes from the inductivist epis- temology of J. M. Keynes the distinction between the positive and negative contents of analogy. Positive analogy consists in the properties and relations that are common to both objects (or systems), whereas negative analogy consists in the dissimilarities between the two 13. Beyond an attempt at formalization, her personal contribution was to define the neutral content of analogy, namely the set of properties or relations shared by the two systems, but also by many others that do not validate the analogy. Hesse was the first to point out the difficulties encountered by this framework for analyzing analogies: in order to evaluate the positive, neutral, and negative con- tents, it is necessary to resort to a weighting of the different properties or relations being compared. However, a distinction must be made between material and formal analogies. Material analogies concern properties or relations that depend on concrete resemblances between objects or systems of objects, whereas formal analogies are established between mathematical formulas that model these properties and relations independently of any material resemblance. Even when it is specified that formal analogies are the ones relevant to science, the oversimplification of the procedure for evaluating analogies has been noted by many epistemologists, among them Leat- herdale 14, who emphasizes that formal analogies are established between models of objects rather than the objects themselves. Leatherdale further insists on the fact that an analogy is always established between relations within models. Simondon adopts 12 Hesse, M., 1963, Models and Analogies in Science, London, Sheed and Ward. 13 Frigg, R., Hartmann, S., 2024, “Models in Science”, in The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Zalta, E. N., Nodelman, U. (eds.). 14 Leatherdale, W. H., 1973, The Role of Models, Metaphors and Analogies in Science, New York, Elsevier.

Progress and Growth 48 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 an equivalent definition (“an analogy is a resemblance of relations and not a relation of resemblance”) 15 and distinguishes between structural analogies, which concern properties and spatial relations, and operational analogies, which concern processes and which alone are valid 16. The respective validity of material, formal, structural, and operational analogies as applied to the technical domain has been examined in Bontems 17. In the case that concerns us, the comparison between technical and organic evolutions also leads to privileging operational analogies and to emphasizing from the outset the importance of the negative content of any possible analogy between biological evolution (as described by Darwinian theory) and technical evolution as analyzed by the “mechanologists.” A first difference is that technical objects, unlike organisms, lack the capacity to reproduce themselves and to generate variability. Seals can produce seal offspring, but forks cannot produce baby forks 18. Genetic drift is a mechanism that can lead to significant consequences in biological evolution, whereas there is no equivalent on the technical side. The industrial “reproduction” of objects is relatively constant and weakly variable. Certainly, technical evolution ex- hibits many cases in which a fortuitous or deliberate modification improving the per- formance of an object is carried over into subsequent “generations,” but this means that such a modification has been incorporated through a modification of production processes. Technical evolution therefore does not present operational analogies with the processes of spontaneous mutation, genetic recombination, or reproduction rates. A second difference is that organic forms are subject to natural selection, which is a mechanical and “blind” process, whereas technical objects can be intentionally selected by human beings. Although some economists 19 draw a parallel between the economic selection of innovations and natural selection, it is necessary to keep in mind the significant differences between the two selection mechanisms. Certainly, biological evolution and technical evolution may display a similar pattern of alter- nation between phases of diversification and selection, as well as between phases of stability or oriented or divergent evolution according to a succession of “punctuated equilibria.” 20 However, the two types of evolution operate on disparate time scales and through radically different mechanisms 21. There is then a third operational difference: unlike what occurs in technical evo- 15 Simondon, G., 2005, L’Individuation à la lumière des notions de forme et d’information, Grenoble, Millon. 16 Simondon, G., 2005, L’Individuation à la lumière des notions de forme et d’information, Grenoble, Millon. 17 Bontems, V., 2017, “Analogies techniques et raisonnements analogiques (une lecture simondonienne)”, in L’Ana- logie dans les techniques, de Beaune, S., HilairePérez, L., Vermeir, K. (eds.), Paris, CNRS Éditions. 18 Lewens, T., 2024, Quatre questions à Tim Lewens, O. Morin. 19 Zuscovitch, E., 1990, “Progrès technique, évolution économique et sélection naturelle”, Revue française d’éco- nomie, 5, pp. 105–134. 20 Gould, S. J., Eldredge, N., 1977, “Punctuated equilibria: the tempo and mode of evolution reconsidered”, Paleo- biology, 3, pp. 115–151. 21 Mokyr, J., 1990, The Lever of Riches: Technological Creativity and Economic Progress, Oxford, Oxford Univer- sity Press.

Silvia de Cesare & Vincent Bontems 49 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 lution, change is irreversible in organic lineages. If an organic form has become entirely extinct (or if another form has succeeded it within a lineage), it cannot natu- rally reappear 22. By contrast, if a technical object is abandoned at a given moment in human history, it may later be rediscovered and reused according to what has been called the “Lazarus effect.” 23 Nothing prevents the reinvention of a vanished object or the reuse of an abandoned process. In other words, the irreversibility of biological evolutions stands in contrast to the omnitemporality of technical possibilities. When Gilbert Simondon applies to technology concepts drawn from the life sci- ences (“lineage,” “hypertely,” “milieu”), this in no way implies that he neglects the negative components of the analogy. In a comparison made by Simondon between technical and biological lineages in On the Mode of Existence of Technical Objects, the philosopher emphasizes the difference between the produced and the generated: “Transposed into biological terms, technical evolution would consist in the fact that a species would produce an organ that would be given to an individual, thereby becoming the first term of a specific lineage which would in turn produce a new or- gan.” 24 This possibility, which is specific to technical evolution, stands in contrast to the constraints of biological evolution, in which the transmission of organs between individual lineages does not exist in the natural state. By contrast, without ignoring the differences, Simondon highlights a common point between technical objects and living beings: both oppose disorder and, ulti- mately, death. In Individuation in the Light of the Notions of Form and Information, Simondon 25 advances the hypothesis that “vital individuation would come to be in- serted into physical individuation by suspending its course, slowing it down, and rendering it capable of propagation in an inchoate state.” 26 He defines the machine as a negentropic organization of matter: “the machine, as a work of organization, is, like life and together with life, that which opposes disorder, the leveling of all things that tends to deprive the universe of powers of change.” 27 Thus, vital individuation as well as technical invention are two becomings of physical individuation that slow down its dissipative process. The machine, like the living being, resists the dissipa- tion of its potentials and maintains, through its exchanges of matter, energy, and in- formation with its milieu, a metastability. In this respect, the machine and the living being do not share the same status as stable and inert inorganic matter. This common point represents, in Simondon’s view, the most important positive component of the analogy. In the case of human living beings, technical evolution 22 We will not discuss here human attempts to counter such irreversibility, notably through socalled “deextinction” efforts involving species such as the woolly mammoth (on this topic, see for example Paganeli, B., Galetti, M., 2025, “DeExtinction at a Crossroads: Ecology, Ethics, and the Future of Conservation in the Biotech Age”, Ecology Letters, 28(9)). 23 Eldredge, N., 2011, “Paleontology and Cornets: Thoughts on Material Cultural Evolution”, Evolution: Education and Outreach, 4, pp. 364–373. 24 Simondon, G., 2013, Du mode d’existence des objets techniques, Paris, Aubier, p. 82 25 Simondon, G., 2005, L’Individuation à la lumière des notions de forme et d’information, Grenoble, Millon. 26 Simondon, G., 2005, L’Individuation à la lumière des notions de forme et d’information, Grenoble, Millon, p. 152. 27 Simondon, G., 2013, Du mode d’existence des objets techniques, Paris, Aubier, p. 18.

Progress and Growth 50 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 constitutes an attempt to obstinately oppose disorder. In both cases, there would therefore be progress when evolution produces individuals that resist entropy more strongly, even though they are produced through very different mechanisms (fab- rication and generation). In both cases, while keeping the dissimilarities in mind, it is possible to speak of lineages. The question that now remains to be analyzed is whether (and in what sense) these two types of evolution involve a progress that can be measured by analogous criteria. 2. Techincal Progress in Simondon This brings us to address question (a) mentioned above: what does progress mean in relation to technical evolution as understood within the perspective of Gil- bert Simondon? To answer this, we will first discuss technical progress within the lineage and the associated milieu; we will then specify what the criteria of technical performance are and in what sense genuine technical progress is not hypertelic. Fi- nally, we will address the question of progress beyond the lineage and the associated milieu. 2.1.“Concretization” and its relativity to “associated milieus” In Simondon28, technical progress is defined as a process of concretization. A lineage begins with the invention of an “abstract individual.” The object is abstract in the sense that its elements are recruited in order to each fulfill a function contrib- uting to the realization of the technical operation, without the totality of the effects of their interactions being anticipated, in particular certain undesirable effects (heating, friction, etc.). The technical individual then “evolves,” that is, its genesis is modified by agents (the restriction of these agents to human beings being open to discussion: animals or artificial intelligences may also intervene). This evolution takes place through a succession of minor advances (partial modifications) and major advances (global reconfigurations). Minor advances consist in modifying a subsystem or an interface in order to attenuate the residual incompatibilities between the different elements that make up the technical system, until its organization becomes “saturated,” that is, until no fur- ther modification can improve its functioning in one respect without degrading it in another. At the time when Simondon produced this analysis, the Soviet engineer Genrich Altshuller arrived at similar conclusions, but by distinguishing more pre- cisely between three types of “contradictions” encountered in technical evolution: the “physical contradiction,” when achieving an improvement would require a pa- rameter to evolve in two opposite directions; the “technical contradiction,” when the improvement of one parameter leads to the degradation of another; and the “coupling contradiction,” when an improvement entails a degradation of the relation to the 28 Simondon, G., 2013, Du mode d’existence des objets techniques, Paris, Aubier.

# Page 8^page=8
Silvia de Cesare & Vincent Bontems 51 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 associated milieu 29. Saturation results from the accumulation of minor advances and requires a ma- jor advance in order to be overcome, that is, a reinvention of the global organization of the technical object. This operation consists in redistributing the various func- tions assigned to the elements, either through a convergence of functions, leading to an increased multifunctionality of the new elements, or through the dissociation of functions previously assigned to a single element. The result is always a more syner- gistic functioning of the individual, but also of the system constituted by this func- tioning together with its associated milieu. And it is in this respect that the crucial distinction lies between genuine progress, which potentially resolves all three types of contradictions, including the coupling contradiction, and a mere improvement in performance. It is necessary to emphasize that the technical individual does not find its con- ditions of existence solely in the internal coherence of its structure with respect to the operation it performs (that is, in becoming progressively less selfdestructive), but also in the relations that this operation maintains with its milieu. This milieu is both natural and artificial. The technical individual inserts itself into this milieu and, through its functioning, contributes to bringing it into existence. The process of con- cretization thus constitutes a progress both toward autocorrelation and toward self- regulation, which amounts to a tendential naturalization of the artificial individual, becoming increasingly similar to a living individual (which is perfectly “concrete”). In Simondon’s words, “the concrete technical object, that is, the evolved technical object, approaches the mode of existence of natural objects: it tends toward inter- nal coherence, toward the closure of the system of causes and effects that operate circularly within its enclosure; moreover, it incorporates a part of the natural world that intervenes as a condition of functioning and thus becomes part of the system of causes and effects.” 30 The progress of technology thus presupposes, in its very definition, an adapta- tion relative to natural conditions that the object transforms—through its own func- tioning or through ancillary dispositifs—so that these conditions constitute its asso- ciated milieu. Now, this circular causality between the technical individual and its associated milieu is not static, since it consists in the coordination between variations in the regime of functioning of technical objects and variations in the associated milieu. Thus, as early as 1958, Simondon arrives at the following precise definition of technical progress: “The necessity of adaptation not to a milieu defined in an exclusive way, but to the function of establishing a relation between two milieus, both of which are themselves evolving, limits adaptation and gives it precision in 29 Altshuller, G., 1999, The Innovation Algorithm. TRIZ, Systemic Invention and Technical Creativity, Worcester, Technical Invention Center. 30 Simondon, G., 2013, Du mode d’existence des objets techniques, Paris, Aubier, p. 56.

Progress and Growth 52 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 the direction of autonomy and concretization. There lies true technical progress” 31. 2.2 Two kinds of improvement in technical performance Let us now try to understand by what criteria one can measure the degree of concretization of the technical individual. Within a technical lineage, the transition between two successive generations of individuals constitutes progress if the cou- pling of the new individuals with their associated milieu is more durable, in the sense that, on the one hand, their functioning is less selfdestructive and, on the other hand, the homeostasis of their associated milieu is maintained. This implies that technical functioning consumes the material and energetic resources of the milieu more spar- ingly and ingeniously extracts information from it, thereby enabling the regulation of its functioning. One then observes that the progress of concretization coincides with the pursuit of efficiency. Abstract individuals make inefficient use of matter, en- ergy, and information; this is why they are both selfdestructive and destructive. This becomes progressively less the case with increasingly concrete individuals. Concret- ization is accompanied by measurable improvements in performance: the technical individual wears out more slowly, achieves higher efficiency, and integrates informa- tion from the milieu more extensively and more effectively. However, it must be emphasized that Simondon insists on the distinction be- tween evolutions that constitute such progress and other evolutions that are also accompanied by improvements in performance but which he designates as “hypertel- ies.” This term, borrowed from biological vocabulary, designates the development of a morphological trait that may become counterproductive—for example, the antlers of deer, whose large size provides advantages (notably in competition for sexual reproduction) but can eventually hinder the animal’s movement. Analogously, tech- nical individuals may be adapted to a given milieu and a particular function in such a way as to achieve superior performance, but at the cost of losing their “genericity” 32: they become more vulnerable to variations in the milieu and less effective for other functions. How can one distinguish between evolutions that are genuinely progressive (processes of concretization) and hypertelic ones? This is not easy to establish on the basis of measuring the performance criteria of the privileged function (key per- formance indicators) within a given milieu. Indeed, in both cases there is an im- provement in specific performance. By contrast, one may assume that the difference becomes manifest as soon as one measures the full set of generic performances of the technical individual. In his course on “Invention and the Development of Tech- niques,” Simondon33 develops a rational classification of machines according to their 31 Simondon, G., 2013, Du mode d’existence des objets techniques, Paris, Aubier, p. 65. 32 Shinn, T., 2008, ResearchTechnology and Cultural Change: Instrumentation, Genericity, Transversality, Oxford, Bardwell Press. 33 Simondon, G., 2005b, L’Invention dans le développement des techniques, Paris, Le Seuil.

Silvia de Cesare & Vincent Bontems 53 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 type of functioning (passive, active, and informational) and their degree—that is, according to the relations between their functioning and the scales within the ob- ject and the associated milieu (structure, microstructure, higherlevel scales). Thus, the solidity of a tool’s handle fitting is a “passive performance of the first degree,” the energetic efficiency of an internal combustion engine is an “active performance of the second degree,” and a computer’s capacity to produce meaning is an infor- mational performance of the third degree. This classification constitutes a universal analytical framework for the generic performances of a technical object 34. It can be represented in the following table: Type / Degree Minor Intermediate Superior Passive 1 Structural qualities E.g.: solidity 2 Material qualities E.g.: resistance 3 Environmental qualities E.g.: stability Active 4 Qualities of internal Mobility E.g.: mechanical efficiency 5 Qualities of ener- gy conversion E.g.: thermal effi- ciency 6 Qualities of exter- nal mobility E.g.: range and amount of work performed (load/dis- tance) Informa- tional 7 Qualities of trans- mission E.g.: speed and fidelity 8 Qualities of am- plification E.g.: sensitivity and resolution 9 Qualities of mean- ing E.g.: processing of complexity through autocorrelation (AI) The work carried out by Guy 35, Guy, Bontems & Minier 36, and by Minier & Bontems 37 confirms that hypertelic evolutions are characterized by the improvement of a single privileged function, often at the expense of other performances, whereas major advances lead to the improvement of several performances, or even of all of them simultaneously. Let us take the example of two cases of hypertelic evolution. The customization of the ultrashortpulse laser (LIBS) of the spectroscopy instrument onboard Curios- ity, a Martian rover, was overadapted to its extraterrestrial environment and, above all, to the conditions of its journey (strong vibrations during launch and landing 34 Bontems, V., 2016, “Sur la classification des objets techniques selon Simondon”, Artefact, 3. 35 Guy, T., 2019, “Relecture mécanologique de la lignée des télescopes”, Artefact, 10, pp. 99–118. 36 Guy, T., Bontems, V., Minier, V., 2019, “Quel laser pour Mars ? (ed.), Paris, Les Belles Lettres. 37 Minier, V., Bontems, V., 2016, “Simondon et l’innovation dans les machines spatiales de l’astronomie”, Nacelles, 6, online.

Progress and Growth 54 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 on Mars). The main improvement concerned a passive criterion of major degree (stability through the damping of disturbances at higher scales), at the expense of its energy efficiency and the fineness of its operations. Conversely, the laser used to study paintings at the Louvre is extremely delicate but not very robust. Whether in the case of the laser onboard Curiosity or in the case of the Louvre laser, both con- stitute hypertelic innovations. Unlike hypertelic evolutions, which represent evolutionary dead ends insofar as the object becomes overadapted to a single function in a single environment, major technical advances (or concretizations) are characterized by an increase in all perfor- mances and by greater functional diversity. In Maunoury’s terms38, the progress of a technical lineage is manifested by a simultaneous improvement of the ‘horizon of feasibility’ and the ‘horizon of creativity.’ Thus, the invention of the maser, followed by that of the laser, and finally of LIBS, represent the crossing of thresholds of con- cretization, with the invention of LIBS making possible both the laser on Curiosity and that of the Louvre. 2.3 Technical progress beyond the lineage and the associated milieu Since the measurement of performance is always relative to the associated en- vironment, and since comparison of the degree of concretization only makes sense within a lineage, it is tempting to conclude that the notion of technical progress has meaning only within a lineage 39 and within a specific cultural context of applica- tion 40. However, Simondon is not satisfied with this restriction: technical progress can- not be reduced to the improvement of a technical scheme; it also involves the inven- tion of new schemes that replace previous ones. He thus indicates that the transition from the lineage of electronic tubes to that of semiconductors constitutes a progress in the ‘pure operational scheme’ of ‘asymmetric conductance.’ 41 This broadens the assessment of progress to an entire family of lineages stemming from the initial invention: ‘one could say that the technical object evolves by generating a family: the original object is the ancestor of this family. One could call such an evolution a natural technical evolution.’ 42 If a technical lineage corresponds to the succession of individuals possessing a technical scheme that carries out the same operation and is subordinated to the same function, the family corresponds to the set of lineages that possess the same ‘pure’ technical scheme—that is, that carry out operations which are certainly different 38 Maunoury, J.L., 1968, La Genèse des innovations : la création technique dans l’activité de la firme, Paris, Presses Universitaires de France. 39 Guchet, X., 2005, Les Sens de l’évolution technique, Paris, Léo Scheer. 40 Basalla, G., 1988, The Evolution of Technology, Cambridge, Cambridge University Press. 41 Simondon, G., 2013, Du mode d’existence des objets techniques, Paris, Aubier, p. 42. 42 Simondon, G., 2013, Du mode d’existence des objets techniques, Paris, Aubier, p. 43.

# Page 12^page=12
Silvia de Cesare & Vincent Bontems 55 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 but are based on the same physical principle of operation. Following Maunoury 43, it should also be specified that this pure scheme must be subordinated to analogous functions; otherwise, the comparison may lose its relevance 44. It remains to be deter- mined to what extent the previous analyses concerning the measurement of technical progress can be transposed to this broadened framework (beyond the lineage and the associated environment) Electronic tubes and semiconductors belong to the same technical family be- cause, even though they do not perform the same operations, they use asymmetric conduction to form chains of ‘logic gates.’ When the first transistor was invented, it performed this function less well than highly perfected electronic tubes, yet it already represented a form of progress. To extend the notion of technical progress to a ‘substitution after saturation’ 45 between lineages within the same family, it must be shown that the new technical scheme offers superior potential performance ac- cording to most criteria. Although the highly concretized object of the first lineage possesses performances superior to those of the abstract object of the new lineage, it also exhibits signs of ‘saturation,’ that is, it can evolve only in a hypertelic manner: any improvement in one type of performance comes at the cost of the degradation of another. Thus, the semiconductor transistor displays a greater potential for evolution than electron tubes, and its lineage did not take long to supplant them46. Sometimes, the two lineages can coexist and even be combined within the same technical system. Thus, in the Herschel satellite one finds two different lineages of bolometers: the his- torical lineage of horn bolometers—robust, perfectly mastered, but saturated—and the innovative lineage of pixel-matrix bolometers 47. In the case of comparing lineages that do not belong to the same family—that is, whose principles of operation are radically different but which nonetheless fulfill the same function (such as a computer and a Babbage machine, in which gears play the role of logic gates)—the difficulty is of a different order. Mere comparison of performance can sometimes be misleading, since hypertelic evolutions also increase certain performances. Ruse 54 is well known for having shown that in Darwin, as well as in many twentiethcentury evolutionary biologists, one can observe the persistence of the idea that evolution entails a change for the better. The American paleontologist Stephen Jay Gould 55 argued that this idea is not at all implied by the very framework (the ‘bare bones’) of evolutionary theory: it persists within biology for extrascien- tific reasons (such as Homo sapiens’ desire to conceive of itself as superior to other organisms), rather than for reasons internal to the theory itself. Recently, the work Organic Progress and Evolutionary Theory 56 has sought to shed light on this issue, which remains a source of controversy to this day. Starting from the observation that a change for the better presupposes an axiological oppo- sition between good and bad, the author examines the meaning of these normative terms and clarifies that, within evolutionary theory, it is possible to assert ‘x is good’ in the sense that ‘x has instrumental value for z.’ This analysis, drawing on the work of Rosenberg and McShea 57, makes it possible to rule out any appeal to value in the sense of final value, in which x would be intrinsically good as an end in itself. This reference to instrumental value allows any notion of good/better in the moral sense to be excluded. De Cesare58 thus proposes to speak of organic value, according to which it makes sense to formulate statements such as ‘an organ is good for a biolog- ical function’ or ‘a biological function is good for the survival and reproduction of organisms.’ Such statements, indeed, make sense in relation to organic performance in a given environment. In the long term, what is ‘better’ for organisms is to be prepared for the potential ‘infidelity of the milieu.’ This property is discussed in contemporary biological literature under the name of ‘evolvability.’ Evolvability applies to different biological systems and at different scales: mi- croevolution, macroevolution, genomes, and clades 79. It is a dispositional concept, since it does not refer to characteristics that are currently in place, but rather to a general disposition to evolve. Evolvability is also necessarily linked to the notion of variability, that is, the disposition to vary. Despite the difficulty of empirically testing whether evolvability does indeed increase over the course of evolution, De Cesare 80 suggests that it can be considered a criterion of global progress, by reference to the conceptual framework proposed by Bourrat, Daeven, and others 81. Without going into the details of this framework, the important point to retain is that the evolutionary success of an organism (which we may call a Type1 organism) in an environment cannot be reduced to the notion of adaptation to a given local environment (the reference environment). A second characteristic that must be taken into account is the robustness of the adaptation, defined as the probability that the Type1 organism will leave descendants (of the same type) in an environment differ- ent from the reference one. But it is also necessary to take evolvability stricto sensu into account: the probability that this organism will generate daughter populations of a different type (Type2), whether in the reference environment or in another one. In short, when these two characteristics are taken into account, it would be reductive to evaluate the evolutionary success of an organism solely by looking at its local adap- tation to a given environment. On the contrary, it is essential to consider the robust- ness of this adaptation and the evolvability potential of the organic form in question. We have seen that, for Simondon, technical progress cannot be reduced to the improvement of a technical scheme; it also involves the invention of new schemes that replace previous ones. Technical progress beyond a single lin- eage would therefore also consist in the fact that each stage of concretization brings about an increase in genericity, that is, in the diversification of the functions that can be assigned to the lineage. Conversely, one can imagine an organic form that gives rise to various populations limited in number but that persist over the long term. Here, one must take into account the relations among several terms: the evolvability of Homo sapiens as a species, technical progress, and growth (both demographic and economic).
